TL;DR: It was a great concept whereupon the execution could be improved.

Ehhh, this is a funny concept, but the execution could have been better in my opinion. A lot of the jokes just were not satisfying to me, and there was no sort of buildup. There were funny parts, though. One in particular that stood out to me was the test log where several anti-viruses were tested, and none of them conflicted, to the amazement of Dr. Smallwood. Also, several Foundation computers having almost melted while performing routine updates is very funny to me.

Overall, I think I'd rate it a 6/10. It was pretty enjoyable, and I certainly didn't hate it. If you ever make another revision (which is probably not likely, seeing as this seems to be from, uh, eight years ago, but still), I, personally, would be excited to read it and see what changed c:

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The problem with intermittent problems is that they are, by nature, intermittent. It may be difficult or impossible to recreate *reliably*. Case in point: the first time I had a power supply die on me. My computer would, at seemingly random intervals, shut off. Sometimes it would be after being on for hours, sometimes Windows wasn't even loaded yet; sometimes it would be during incredibly heavy loads, sometimes it was when it was sitting idle with nothing running but background stuff. It turned out that there had been a small bit of… Something wrong with one of the wires, I honestly can't remember now if it was corrosion or pinched or loose or what. What was happening was that, due to vibrations, it would *very* occasionally wiggle just right to short out; once we found that, if I had been capable (or willing) to run it with the power supply open and exposed, I could have recreated it every time, but there was no way to actually tell before hand.

THAT, is where the seemingly random, intermittent problems most usually come from. Not a part that's *failed*, but one that is just on the very edge of complete failure.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
From where I sit, which is in a network operations center, where my job is to watch for alerts for all sorts of software, networking, and hardware errors from datacenters full of servers, computers act up for many, many reasons, most of which can be abstracted to, operating environments are dynamic, not static. The hard drive that was 84% full is now 85% full. Something changed the boot order since the last reboot, so that one application tried to pull a config file down from another server before the network connection was up. That Web server is responding slowly, because an application is indexing the documents and using a lot of disk I/O.

I was making a joke above about system logs. Look at the system logs for any system that's apparently running smoothly, and see how many warnings and error messages there are. Operating systems are complex and messy, and sometimes processes conflict with each other or run out of storage space.

item.content:encoded:
Doping imputities make each circuit unique on a molecular level, and it's not even uncommon for impurities to cause a circuit to malfunction. But that circuit will malfunction the same way every time. A given electrical current passes through a particular medium in a certain way, it can't change it's path and pattern anymore than the sun can set in the west.

Dopant migration is one of those things that's technically true, but doesn't mean what it seems to. The details are very boring, but suffice to say that recreating data from dopant migration is like recreating all the e-mails you've ever written by examing the wear patterns on your fingerprints from the keyboard. Theoretically, it's possible, but mind-blowingly unlikely.

I get what you're saying about the programming errors though. Point of view matters. I just don't think that way about it because I spend so much time working at the machine code level. The programmer is just some other user that messed with my machine before I got to it.

Like I said up-thread, I think I'm just the wrong audience for this.

An ex, who was really into computer stuff, once told me that there are stochastic processes even in the most reliable hardrware (and that each modern circuit is unique due to, uhhh… let me recall the quote, "random operational parameter fluctuations due to presence of randomly distributed dopant atoms". Also, migration of dopant atoms in memory chippery due to particular usage patterns is kinda a big thing with paranoid "spy tech" boffins, some guy had an article about recovering data from "dopant migration imprints", I think (which is kinda crazy, but if you're curious, I can phone my ex and try to find out the names of relevant papers)

Also, some types of programming errors cause what can can be, from "user side" of things, pretty hard to distinguish from a classic description of intermittent glitch (they will eventually be reproduced, but that's a bit of a cold comfort when you face something that was "wrong a moment ago, but right now" ;-) )

item.content:encoded:
I think I might just be the wrong audience for this joke, because I work with both PCs and hand-cobbled circuitry daily.

It has been proven to me time and time again, to the point where I can't deny it, that when a bit of electronics is "acting up" it is always an ID/OT error. That is, the problem exists between the keyboard and the chair. GIGO, and other cliche tech support tropes.

Circuits and programs always do the same thing, they have no choice. You get different results because humans are not designed for precision work, we only think we do the same thing every time because our minds are as fuzzy as that forgotten slice of pizza under the couch. Computers do only what we tell them to do, not what we meant to tell them to do.
